source.title: How Far Can Sharpness and Complexity Jointly Explain Generalization?
source.authors: Ziyu Cheng; Xi-Tong Zhang; Longxiu Huang; Rong-Rong Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures sharpness and complexity metrics against training–test generalization gaps using Pareto ordering and regression, a different evaluation of the relationship in V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results for sharpness–complexity pairs and single-factor metrics. The rows below select illustrative table results; values used to select training runs or metric definitions are not results.
record.test_reason: The single-factor analyses test whether magnitude-scaled perturbation sensitivity tracks generalization gaps among well-trained convolutional networks. They use loss increases and adaptive Hessian statistics rather than V7's perturbation tolerance before training error rises. Joint sharpness–complexity results do not establish the predictive value of sharpness alone.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: suitably chosen sharpness–complexity pairs explain gap ordering in many evaluated settings; finite perturbation scales often help, function norm is comparatively robust, and remaining failures leave open whether refined metrics or additional factors are needed.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures adaptive-Hessian sharpness and several complexity representations against generalization gaps using Pareto analysis and regression; it does not reproduce the magnitude-aware perturbation-tolerance comparison described in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported explanatory power changes with perturbation scale, complexity representation, architecture, optimizer, and pooled versus individual setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Sharpness paired with function norm gives strong joint ordering in the selected CIFAR-10 settings, but substantially weaker ordering for CIFAR-100 WideResNet without batch normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suitable combinations of magnitude-aware sharpness and function-level complexity jointly track loss generalization gaps in many, but not all, trained-network populations.

record.problems: The metrics and evaluation tools are probes rather than a direct test of a causal mechanism. Results vary by architecture and metric choice; the authors identify WideResNet no-BN as a poorly explained regime. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the table values.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 4, 5, and 7 report many additional metric-pair outcomes across architectures, optimizers, datasets, and pooled settings; Appendix Tables 9, 11, and 13 report additional single-factor outcomes. These are omitted to keep the selection focused on representative strong and weak comparisons relevant to V7.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the role of local connectivity.
Held-out optimizer performance under matched tuning budgets; comparing metric correlations across optimizers does not test this.
Batch-size penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their recovery.

The original perturbation tolerance before training error rises, training–test error gaps, comparisons against margin measures, and SVHN. The supplied text does not establish the original no-augmentation condition.
Retraining after removal of memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Additional single-factor results and norm comparisons are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing entries. Joint PCR and single-factor CR use different pair denominators; their numerical difference alone does not establish improvement on the same comparisons. Excerpt E2 concerns parameter-norm pairs, whereas its linked rows R1 and R3 concern function-norm pairs. No verdict establishes causation.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Generalization as network width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture performance.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization under tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch generalization under epoch budgets.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.

The paper does not test perturbation tolerance as a stand-alone sharpness measure, compare against margin measures, or report SVHN results. Its results concern adaptive Hessian sharpness paired with selected complexity metrics, across CIFAR-10/100 settings.
Effects of removing memorized training examples.

rows.subject: ResNet18 no-BN sgd
rows.stage_stated: trained; well-trained models retained at training loss ≤ 0.01
rows.operation_detail: Measured Pareto contradiction rate and linear-regression R² for adaptive finite-scale trace sharpness paired with function norm.
rows.note: Lower PCR indicates fewer violations of the expected metric-to-gap ordering; both regression coefficients are positive.
rows.check: Numbers and conditions match Table 4, but PCR 1.5% and R² 0.85 assess a joint sharpness–function-norm predictor. They cannot establish V7's single-factor relationship or superiority over norm measures.

rows.subject: ResNet18 no-BN sgd
rows.stage_stated: trained; well-trained models retained at training loss ≤ 0.01
rows.operation_detail: Measured Pareto contradiction rate and linear-regression R² for infinitesimal trace sharpness paired with function norm.
rows.note: Compared with R1, this pair has a higher contradiction rate and lower R², though the ordering remains relatively consistent.
rows.check: Numbers match Table 4. This joint predictor cannot isolate sharpness's relationship with the gap. Its slightly weaker performance than R1 does not itself constitute a partial V7 effect.

rows.subject: VGG13 no-BN sgd
rows.stage_stated: trained; well-trained models retained at training loss ≤ 0.01
rows.operation_detail: Measured Pareto contradiction rate and linear-regression R² for adaptive finite-scale trace sharpness paired with function norm.
rows.note: The paper describes finite-scale sharpness with function norm as showing strong explanatory power in this setting.
rows.check: Numbers and conditions match Table 4, but the joint predictor's success cannot establish that sharpness alone tracks gaps.

rows.subject: VGG13 no-BN sgd
rows.stage_stated: trained; well-trained models retained at training loss ≤ 0.01
rows.operation_detail: Measured Pareto contradiction rate and linear-regression R² for infinitesimal top-eigenvalue sharpness paired with function norm.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this result with finite-scale top-eigenvalue sharpness, which has PCR 4.3% and R² 0.85.
rows.check: Numbers match Table 4. The authors describe both this pair and its finite-scale counterpart as strongly explanatory; the extraction's partial state rests only on their relative performance. Neither isolates V7's sharpness effect.

rows.subject: WideResNet no-BN sgd
rows.stage_stated: trained; well-trained models retained at training loss ≤ 0.01
rows.operation_detail: Measured Pareto contradiction rate and linear-regression R² for adaptive finite-scale trace sharpness paired with function norm.
rows.locator: Table 4, CIFAR-100 WideResNet no-BN sgd; Observation 8
rows.note: The authors identify this architecture as the only exception to their observation that nearly every evaluated setting has at least one strongly explanatory pair.
rows.check: Numbers match Table 4, including the negative sharpness coefficient. They diagnose a weak, directionally inconsistent joint predictor, not the single-factor relationship named in V7.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10, SGD-trained ResNet18 without batch normalization; single-factor finite-scale adaptive trace at σ = 0.50
relationships.reason: R7 shows a positive but incomplete relationship (CR 19.1%, R² 0.53); Table 9's function norm performs better (CR 16.2%, R² 0.72), limiting the ranking-superiority component under this alternative measurement.
relationships.display_finding: Finite-scale adaptive trace explained some variation in loss gaps (R² = 0.53). The available evidence does not confirm its reported disadvantage relative to function norm.

relation.reason: Own single-factor results measure whether adaptive sharpness orders generalization gaps among well-trained convolutional models and compare its explanatory power with complexity metrics.

tranche.reason: Tests sharpness–gap association and comparative ranking using magnitude-scaled finite-loss perturbations, contradiction ratios and regression, differing from V7's training-error perturbation tolerance.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase matches the abstract and conclusion. The study measures loss gaps and finite-scale loss sensitivity; V7's training-error tolerance and margin-measure comparison remain untested.
